description: We are Team Recursive, building FarmShift Nepal. Our platform uses NASA Earth observation data to help Nepali farmers make climate-informed crop-planning decisions. We welcome teammates interested in AI/ML, data analysis, Earth science, agriculture, GIS, web development, UI/UX, and data visualization. Join us to use science and technology to solve real agricultural challenges in Nepal!
summary:
FarmShift is a free, bilingual (English/नेपाली) web app that turns NASA Earth observations into simple farm decisions for smallholder farmers in Nepal. A farmer picks a location, enters farm size and basic soil information, and FarmShift pulls five years of daily NASA POWER climate data (MERRA-2 and CERES) plus near-real-time NASA GIBS satellite layers (SMAP soil moisture, GPM IMERG rainfall, MODIS land surface temperature), and combines them with a 7-day forecast.

It then provides: (1) crop rotations ranked from 36 Nepali crops by temperature, rainfall, water balance and elevation, never repeating a plant family in a row; (2) fertilizer and lime doses for Urea, DAP and MOP in local units (Ropani, Bigha); (3) a 4-week task plan that warns against fertilizing before heavy rain or on waterlogged soil; and (4) an assistant that answers from curated NARC and MoALD guidance and cites the source.
details:
FarmShift is a web-based tool that's free to use for farmers or local agriculture workers in Nepal to make informed farming decisions. FarmShift integrates NASA satellite data and short-term weather forecasts with local government agricultural guidance from Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC). A farmer can explore their next crop rotation recommendations, precise fertilizer recommendations (for their local land unit such as Ropani, Bigha), a 4-week task calendar, and warnings of heavy rainfall & risk of floods.

1. What does it do? / How does it work?

FarmShift is a web-based tool that works right in your browser, requiring no sign up.

As you open the app, you choose a location in Nepal. You give your farm size. You can also give some basic info about your soil (like soil texture, pH, last season crop you planted).

This app will do four things:

  1. a) Fetch climate/weather data: This app fetches historical temperature, rainfall and soil moisture data from the NASA POWER database. It displays real-time satellite maps from NASA GIBS. It pulls a 7-day local weather forecast from Open-Meteo.
  2. b) Recommends crop rotations: Takes into account local climate, elevation, and water availability to suggest what to plant next. Ensures we don't recommend the same family of plants in a row, naturally breaking the pest and disease cycles.
  3. c) Calculates soil and fertilizer needs: Translates normal soil science into bags and kilograms of common fertilizers in Nepal (Urea, DAP, MOP) and whether or not they need agricultural lime for acidic soil.
  4. d) Makes a 4-week to-do list: Makes a simple weekly checklist (when to sow, when to weed, when to fertilize). If the weather forecast shows a heavy downpour or there is saturated soil from satellite data, it will warn the farmer to not spread fertilizer yet so it won't be washed away.

2. What are the benefits?

  1. a) Saves money and reduces waste of fertilizers: Many farmers guess or over-use Urea because it's subsidized. FarmShift can calculate the exact balance needed, considering the existing nitrogen in DAP and previous crops like legumes.
  2. b) It takes into consideration the climate, elevation, and water availability to suggest what to plant next and it makes sure we don't recommend the same family of plants in a row, naturally breaking the pest and disease cycles.
  3. c) Speaks the farmers' language: The whole app is switchable between English and Nepali with one click. It also uses traditional land measurements (Ropani, Bigha) in Nepal, not just hectares and acres.
  4. d) Weather smart scheduling: It combines space-age soil moisture data from satellite and 7-day rain prediction. This gives early warning for waterlogging to safeguard seeds and inputs to farmers.

3. What's the intended impact going to be?

We want to bring the power of space-grade satellite data to the regular usage of agriculture in Nepal.

In general, Nepalese farmers have a small plot of land, and they face unpredictable monsoon rain, drastic elevation changes and degraded soil. Advanced satellite data is available, but often it lies around in research papers and complex government portals and is hard to use for common people. FarmShift is a way to bridge the gap. We want to bring pragmatic and localized recommendations to farmers and local agriculture extension officers, to reduce crop loss, improve soil health and increase the seasonal yield.

4. What are the tools that were used to build the project? (coding language, hardware, software, etc.)

Frontend and Programming Language: TypeScript, React 18, Vite, Tailwind CSS

Maps and Visualization: Leaflet, loading layers from NASA EOSDIS GIBS (satellite data: soil moisture, precipitation and surface temperature).

Data Sources & APIs:

  1. NASA POWER API - long-term solar, rainfall & agroclimatology data.
  2. NASA EOSDIS GIBS - live satellite tile data (SMAP, GPM IMERG, MODIS).
  3. Open-Meteo API - accurate 7-day rainfall and temperature forecast.
  4. OpenStreetMap Nominatim - search for districts & municipalities (Nepal).
  5. Agronomic Knowledge Base - official crop and fertilizer standard manuals from Nepal Agricultural Research Council (NARC) and Ministry of Agriculture and Livestock Development (MoALD).

Testing and Development:

  1. Vitest - for automated unit tests (we have 30 unit tests for our calculation formulas and our rotation logic).
  2. Git/GitHub - version control.

5. How is the project creative?

  1. a) Client side everything: Most apps that handle satellite data work with expensive Python cloud servers or paid backends. Our algorithms and data retrieval pipeline are entirely implemented in the user's browser, so it's completely free and fast even on low-end devices.
  2. b) Translating NASA data to reality: Instead of showing plain satellite graphs which mean nothing to a normal farmer, FarmShift translates it into actions (e.g. "Wait 2 days before adding fertilizer since rain is coming" or "Add 75 kg of lime per Ropani since your soil is too acidic").
  3. c) Pest-smart rotation: Instead of the simple test of whether a crop can be grown in a specific temperature, our rotation logic takes botanical family into account to prevent related crops being planted in succession, to naturally reduce pests and soil exhaustion.
  4. d) Use of a RAG model: Our project uses a simple RAG model that gives the farmer information on specific topics. The answers come only from the agriculture handbooks and show their source, so it can't make up answers.

6. What are the considerations made by the team?

  1. a) Extremely different terrain in Nepal: Nepal has a very short distance from low flat areas (60 m elevation) to the Himalaya. Obviously there are dramatic changes in weather and suitability of crops from one valley to another. We took altitude and local micro-climates directly into consideration for making the recommendations.
  2. b) Acidic soil and chemical imbalance: Large areas of Nepal's farmland have acidic soil (pH < 5.5) that traps nutrients. We made sure to add formulas to calculate the lime needed to correct acidic soil. Thus, farmers don't spend money on the wrong fertilizer if the soil is not able to receive it properly.
  3. c) Accessibility and rural internet: Rural areas sometimes have slow or patchy internet. We focused on making the app light, avoiding heavy server calls, making it work smoothly on mobile screens, and completely translating it to Nepali.
  4. d) Accuracy and safety: We didn't want an AI throwing out random or unsafe farming advice. So the on-board RAG assistant uses verified NARC and MoALD agriculture handbooks to base its answers on proven/tested agriculture.
